title: Can People Truly Change?
rootClaim: Human personality, core character traits, and behavioral patterns are capable of fundamental, permanent transformation throughout an individual's lifetime.

branches.text: Neuroplasticity demonstrates that the adult brain continuously rewires its neural pathways in response to deliberate practice, environment, and therapy.

children.text: Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) and targeted neuro-feedback structurally alter amygdala reactivity and prefrontal cortex connectivity over time.
Neural Set-Point Theory: Genetic hardwiring establishes baseline affective ranges to which individuals inevitably return following temporary interventions (hedonic adaptation).
Epigenetics reveals that environmental stimuli and sustained behavioral shifts can modify gene expression without changing underlying DNA sequences.
Epigenetic changes are constrained by canalization, where developmental buffers resist extreme phenotypic departures from baseline genetic profiles.
Post-Traumatic Growth: Extreme narrative identity shocks can trigger sudden, enduring shifts in core values and worldview.

branches.text: Empirical longitudinal studies show high rank-order stability in Big Five personality traits across decades of adulthood.

children.text: Five-Factor Model stability coefficients (e.g., Introversion vs Extraversion, Neuroticism) remain remarkably constant after age 30.
Maturity Principle: While rank-order stability remains high, mean-level personality changes systematically show increased Conscientiousness and Agreeableness across the lifespan.
Mean-level changes reflect social role adaptation (e.g., career, parenting) rather than fundamental shifts in underlying emotional temperament.
High Recidivism Rates: Chronic behavioral patterns like antisocial traits or addictive compulsions exhibit strong relapse tendencies despite clinical intervention.
Environmental Recurrence Bias: Recidivism stems primarily from returning to un-changed socio-economic environments rather than inherent biological immutability.

branches.text: Existentialist Epistemology: Human consciousness is characterized by radical freedom (existence precedes essence), making static self-definition a form of 'bad faith'.

children.text: Jean-Paul Sartre's radical freedom asserts that individuals continuously re-create their character through current choices rather than past determinants.
Psychological Determinism: Conscious choices are downstream manifestations of unconscious automatic processing and childhood attachment schemas.

definitions.description: The capacity of the nervous system to modify its structural organization and functional neural pathways in response to experience and learning.
The taxonomy of five broad personality dimensions: Openness, Conscientiousness, Extraversion, Agreeableness, and Neuroticism (OCEAN).
The empirical psychological observation that individuals generally become more socially dominant, agreeable, conscientious, and emotionally stable as they age.
A measure of the ability of a population or genome to produce the same phenotype regardless of variability of its environment or underlying genotype.
Sartrean existential concept where an individual adopts false values and disowns their inherent freedom to choose who they are.
